ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Markers — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces markers through the card’s activity — making bold colourful lines — and teaches the two marker disciplines: the cap goes back on, and the line goes all the way.

What is this?

Markers are tubes of liquid ink with a felt tip: touch paper and color flows out with no pressure at all. They make the boldest, smoothest lines in the drawer.

What does it mean?

Bold lines teach commitment — a marker line cannot be erased, so the child learns to move with intention. Line variety (straight, wavy, zigzag) is also pre-writing: letters are just lines that learned manners.

What does the child need to know?

Washable markers, paper with a backing sheet underneath (markers travel through), and the cap rule: finished means capped. Thick tips for small hands, thin tips for details.

Why this matters

Markers give maximum result for minimum strength, which makes them the confidence tool of the drawer — the picture always shows up. The cap ritual, practiced daily, is responsibility in miniature.

What it teaches

Intentional stroke control, line vocabulary (straight, wavy, zigzag, loop), cap discipline, hand strength for the cap click, and sound-symbol play — lines that make noise.

Words to learn

markercapboldlinestraightwavyzigzagsweep

Say this to your child

“"Markers! Cap off — CHEK! Now one bold line, all the way across — don’t stop! Another one, wiggly like a river. Now sharp like lightning — zigzag, zigzag! What sound does YOUR line make?"”

Step by step

  1. Pop the cap together — CHEK! — and name the ceremony.
  2. Draw one long straight line across the whole page without stopping.
  3. Draw a wavy line, then a zigzag — say each one out loud as it lands.
  4. Play the sound game: hum the straight line, drum the zigzag, sing the wave.
  5. Cap it together before the paper changes — the line ends, the cap clicks, done.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, three orange markers stand side by side with their caps on — capped is their resting state, and the whole lesson starts by popping one off.

Ask your child

"What goes back on when we finish?" (the cap) "Can we erase a marker line?" (no — that is why we mean it) "Draw me a zigzag in the air." "Which line sounds like a drum?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may cap every marker with a satisfying click and line them up like crayons, draw sound effects on purpose, or narrate each line — "this one is a ROAR" — which is a sound effects department being born.

Out in the real world

Street painters and sign makers use wide markers for big bold letters, and warehouses mark floors with them. Bold lines that survive outdoors all come from the same felt-tip idea.

Try it together

Line orchestra: lay three long papers on the floor, one per line type. Walk the papers and play each line — stomp the zigzag, glide the wave. The marker game becomes a whole-body concert.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do when we finish a marker?" (cap it) "Show me a bold line." "Name two kinds of lines." (straight, wavy, zigzag — any two)

This lesson pairs with the Markers flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.
